bib.title: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Program Better

question: Can a code LM generate its own programming problems and solutions, filter them with a Python interpreter, and improve its own held-out test performance by fine-tuning on them?
hypothesis: Interpreter-verified synthetic puzzle-solution pairs generated by an LM are instructive enough to improve that LM; larger generators give more diverse, more useful data.
contributions: A procedure that generates diverse programming puzzles with solutions verified correct and efficient by execution
Release of datasets of 1M synthetic puzzles and solutions plus source code
Evidence that the problems are instructive: the generating LM improves on held-out test problems

method.summary: Few-shot prompt an LM with random training puzzles (no solutions) to propose new puzzles, filter trivial/invalid ones, have the LM attempt solutions with the P3 medium few-shot prompt, verify with the Python interpreter (keep up to 8 shortest correct solutions per puzzle), then fine-tune on the verified pairs and repeat. Four 1M-pair datasets are generated (Codex, Neo-125M, 1.3B, 2.7B) and each Neo size is fine-tuned on each for one epoch.
method.task: Self-improvement on Python programming puzzles (P3) via synthetic data with execution-based verification

datasets.name: P3 train puzzles
datasets.source: Python Programming Puzzles repo (Schuster et al. 2021)
datasets.preprocessing: Used as few-shot prompt seeds; a median of 43 puzzles per Codex prompt

datasets.name: P3 test puzzles
datasets.source: P3; 150 of them derived from HumanEval

datasets.name: Verified synthetic datasets (Codex, Neo-125M, Neo-1.3B, Neo-2.7B)
datasets.size: 1M puzzle-solution pairs each; 74M, 65M, 66M, 98M tokens for Neo-125M/1.3B/2.7B/Codex-generated per Table 1 (Verified-125M 74M, Verified-1.3B 65M, Verified-2.7B 66M, Verified-Codex 98M)
datasets.source: Generated by the LMs; iteration 1 produced 25K unique pairs per Neo model, iteration 2 produced 1M
datasets.preprocessing: Dedup, type-hint validity, parse check, trivial-solution filter (about half of generated puzzles removed); a=128 solution attempts, 1 s timeout judge, up to m=8 shortest distinct correct solutions per puzzle

datasets.name: Human
datasets.size: 635 solutions to 95 of the 155 train puzzles, 74K tokens
datasets.source: Codex-written solutions verified as in the pipeline

models.name: GPT-Neo 125M / 1.3B / 2.7B
models.architecture: GPT-3-like transformer, pretrained on the Pile

models.name: Codex (Davinci, Cushman)
models.architecture: GPT-3-like transformer trained on code, accessed via API

other.note: Not fine-tuned; used for generation, as a comparison, and for 2048-d code embeddings

training.objective: Supervised fine-tuning on interleaved puzzle, solution and assert text mirroring the few-shot solving prompt (Fig 9 format)
training.epochs: 1 epoch per fine-tuning run (12 runs: 3 Neo sizes x 4 datasets); up to 10-11 epochs in Fig 14/15 study
training.tokens: 1 epoch of Codex-verified data is about 92M tokens (Fig 16 caption); 11 epochs is over 1 billion tokens

other.iterations: n=1 for Codex (1M); n=2 for Neo models (25K then 1M), stopped at 2 for cost
other.note: Whether fine-tuning restarts from the base model or continues each iteration is not stated

inference.temperature: 0.9 when solving puzzles to build fine-tuning data; 0.8 when testing fine-tuned models (sweep at 0.2 steps found 0.8 optimal for Pass@100)
inference.samples: 256 candidate solutions per test puzzle; Pass@k for k=1..100 with the unbiased estimator of Chen et al. 2021; a=128 attempts per synthetic puzzle when generating data
inference.prompting: Puzzle generation: random train puzzles concatenated without solutions, LM completes with new ones (median 43 puzzles for Codex). Solving and testing: P3 medium prompt, five fixed puzzle/solution examples plus the target puzzle (few-shot, k=5)

parameters.trivial_filter: int in -10..100, fixed float, str and list probes; all bool puzzles deemed trivial

other.diversity_embedding: OpenAI Codex code embeddings, 2048-d, 10,000 puzzle sample per dataset; UMAP default with densmap=True; K-means (sklearn defaults) with C=4..64 clusters fit on 397 P3 puzzles; entropy metric averaged over 10 runs; seed 0 for C=8 table

metrics.name: Pass@k
metrics.definition: Fraction of test puzzles with a correct solution within k sampled attempts (Chen et al. 2021 unbiased estimator from 256 samples)

metrics.name: Cluster entropy
metrics.definition: Entropy of distribution of dataset puzzles over C K-means clusters

baselines: Neo fine-tuned on 635 human-set Codex solutions
Neo fine-tuned on unverified Codex data
eval.protocol: Few-shot on 228 P3 test puzzles; headline numbers are Pass@100 for Neo-2.7B after 1 epoch; no seeds or confidence intervals reported

evidence.quote: The ﬁxed temperature of 0.9 from prior work [Schuster et al., 2021] was used in all puzzle-solving for generating ﬁne-tuning data, where temperature of 0.8 was used for testing the ﬁne-tuned model

results.claim: Fine-tuning Neo-2.7B on 1M Codex-generated interpreter-verified puzzles for one epoch raises Pass@100 from 7.5% to 38.2%.
results.setup: Neo-2.7B, 228 P3 test puzzles, 1 epoch on Verified-Codex
results.table: Table 1, row Verified-Codex, column Pass@100 (baseline row 7.5%)
results.note: Table 3 reports an overall improvement factor of 4.95 (not 38.2/7.5 = 5.09)

results.claim: Neo-2.7B fine-tuned on its own 1M verified synthetic pairs reaches 20.6% Pass@100 versus 7.5% baseline.
Verified data is much more valuable than unverified: Unverified-Codex gives 21.5% versus 38.2% for Verified-Codex.
results.setup: Neo-2.7B, 1M Codex pairs with and without interpreter filtering, 1 epoch (value is the unverified case, baseline_value the verified case)

results.claim: Data from larger generators helps more, even a 125M generator helps the 2.7B model (15.4% vs 7.5%).
results.quote: performance of Neo-2.7B improves even when trained on code generated by Neo-125M because the Neo-125M data has been ﬁltered by a Python interpreter for correctness

results.claim: Fine-tuning on only 635 human-set solutions improves Pass@100 modestly to 10.5%.
Test accuracy more than doubles from self-generated data in publicly available LMs.
results.quote: In experiments on publicly-available LMs, test accuracy more than doubles.

results.claim: Iteration 2 (1M samples) adds little over iteration 1 (25K samples), so the pipeline was stopped at n=2.
results.quote: Small gains in iteration 2 suggest that performance may have plateaued.

results.claim: Cluster entropy (C=8) is higher for larger generators: Codex 2.69, Neo-2.7B 2.60, Neo-1.3B 2.45, Neo-125M 2.28 (P3 human 2.85).
results.setup: 10,000 puzzle sample per dataset, K-means fit on 397 P3 puzzles, Codex embeddings; value shown is Neo-125M
results.table: Appendix D table, row Neo-125M, column Entropy

results.claim: Fine-tuned Neo still does better few-shot than zero-shot even after 11 epochs (over 1 billion tokens).
results.quote: Across all 3 model sizes, testing Neo in few-shot beats zero-shot signiﬁcantly even after 11 epochs of ﬁne-tuning

results.claim: Temperature 0.8 maximised Pass@100 in a sweep with step 0.2.
results.setup: All three Neo sizes, 1 epoch (about 92M tokens)
results.quote: verified that 0.8 was also optimal for our model and dataset at a 0.2 search step size

results.claim: Overall improvement factor on test puzzles is 4.95; gains are largest on trivial inverse (1.34 to 8.47).
results.setup: Fine-tuned vs baseline Neo, per P3 domain; model and dataset for this table not stated in caption
results.quote: The overall test performance improved by a 4.95 factor.

results.claim: Roughly half of generated puzzles are eliminated by pre-filtering; fewer than 1% are duplicates.
results.quote: approximately half of the generated puzzles were eliminated

limits: Fine-tuning hyperparameters (optimizer, learning rate, batch size, hardware, compute, seeds) are not reported; no confidence intervals.
Only tested on programming puzzles with a deterministic verifier; authors note this is unavailable for most domains.
Gains plateau by iteration 2; authors suggest RL for generation and filtering as future work.
No test of transfer to English-to-code tasks; authors warn of catastrophic forgetting of natural language.
Codex could not be fine-tuned, so self-improvement is shown only for Neo; Codex data is cross-model distillation plus interpreter filtering.
Synthetic puzzles are shorter and closer to the training set than the test set (distance 0.249 vs 0.302 for Neo-125M), a mild train-distribution overfit.
Many generated puzzles are uninteresting or flawed (unused variables, misused concepts), per hand inspection in Appendix F.
Judge is not a full sandbox.

terms.definition: A verification function f(., x); a solution is g(x) such that f(g(x), x) = True
Learning from the Python interpreter's correctness filtering, as distinct from knowledge distillation from a larger model
